messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 67-year-old widowed military medic who came to treatment after years of telling himself he should be able to handle what happened on the road. He had spent much of his adult life in situations where injury, blood, and sudden death were part of the work, and he had built a sense of himself around staying steady when others could not. The collision that now returns to him did not happen in combat but on an ordinary drive, which is part of what still unsettles him. He remembers the violent interruption of a normal day: the abrupt impact, the crushed metal, the smell that flooded the vehicle, and the terrifying recognition that he might die there. What stands out most sharply is not a tidy sequence but fragments that arrive with force—the sharp odor of alcohol on the other driver, the burnt smell after impact, and the sounds inside the wreck, which he still hears in his head when the memory breaks through.

When he tries to describe the crash in session, David often begins in a clear, matter-of-fact way and then loses the thread. He will pause, stare past the therapist, and say that it gets slippery at exactly the point where he tries to put the whole thing together. He knows there was the hit, the smell, the noise, the fear, but the account does not stay organized long enough for him to finish it. At times he speaks about the memory as if it happened to someone else, saying it feels oddly detached from him, as though he were handed another man’s scene to carry around. Yet the sensory pieces are immediate. If he passes a crash on the road, even at a distance, he does not just think about his own collision; he is back in contact with the image of smashed cars and with the sounds he heard that day. The smell of alcohol on someone’s breath can change him instantly. Burnt odors, even brief ones in everyday life, make his body react before he has time to tell himself where he is.

In the months after the collision, David began shaping his life around not setting these reactions off. He stopped driving, and he also stopped being a passenger whenever he could avoid it. For a man used to competence and mobility, this has narrowed his world considerably. Practical tasks now require planning around rides, postponement, or simply deciding not to go. In vehicles he feels trapped and alert, bracing at ordinary traffic sounds and jolting at noises that other people barely register. Those around him have noticed how quickly he jumps. His body reacts hard when he is reminded of the crash—his heart surges, his muscles tense, and he feels as though danger has arrived again without warning.

He also began policing his own mind. Because the memory can feel fragmented and unreal, David has come to watch his thoughts closely for any sign that he is “going crazy.” He pays attention to whether an image has come into his head, whether a sound in memory has started up again, whether he is losing his place. At the same time, he tries hard not to think about the crash at all. He cuts off reminders internally, pushes the scene away, and attempts to shut down anything connected to it. This leaves him in a constant bind: scanning for signs in his own mind while trying to force the subject out of awareness.

What weighs heavily on him is the meaning he has given the collision and his response to it. David speaks about the crash as something that happened because of the way he acted. Even without offering a full coherent account, he circles back to what he should have done differently and whether a better man would have prevented it. He has begun to doubt his judgment more broadly, saying he cannot trust himself to do the right thing. For someone whose identity was built around making correct decisions under pressure, this has cut deeply. He does not speak about himself with sympathy; he says instead that his reaction shows he is weak.

He finally sought help after recognizing how small his life had become and how much effort each day was taking. The immediate push came from the accumulation of ordinary moments he could no longer manage easily: the sight of accident-damaged cars on the road, the sudden hit of alcohol on someone nearby, the burnt smell of something overheating, the jolt of everyday sounds that made his whole body react. He arrived wanting, in his words, to be able to tell what happened without disappearing in the middle of it. What frightens him most is the possibility that he can no longer trust his own mind or himself in a crisis. What he hopes for, more quietly, is to recover some sense that the man who survived that crash is still recognizably him.
